title: Texas measles cases hit 561: Here's how it spreads and how to stay safe

content:
Texas health officials report 561 confirmed measles cases in the state. Public health agencies are urging residents to check vaccination status, avoid large gatherings if unvaccinated, and seek medical guidance if symptoms appear. Local health departments are ramping up testing, contact tracing and vaccination clinics to limit further transmission.

How measles spreads
Measles is one of the most contagious viral diseases. It transmits through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes, but viral particles can also linger in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours in an enclosed space. An infected person can spread the virus from about four days before the rash appears to four days after.

Symptoms and timeline
Initial symptoms typically include high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Small white spots inside the mouth (Koplik spots) can appear before a red, blotchy rash that usually starts on the face and spreads downward. The incubation period is generally 7 to 14 days after exposure, which means cases may continue to appear for weeks without rapid intervention.

Prevention and vaccination
The primary protection against measles is the MMR vaccine, given in two doses. One dose is about 93% effective; two doses are about 97% effective. Public health authorities recommend that children receive the first dose at 12–15 months and the second at 4–6 years, with catch-up schedules for older children and adults who are not fully vaccinated. High vaccination coverage is essential for community (herd) immunity.

Post-exposure steps
If someone is exposed and not fully vaccinated, a timely MMR shot within 72 hours of exposure can provide protection or reduce severity. For certain high-risk people (infants, pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals), immune globulin may be recommended if given within a limited window after exposure. Anyone who develops symptoms should isolate and contact a healthcare provider before visiting clinics or emergency rooms to avoid exposing others.

Practical advice for residents
- Check vaccination records and get missing MMR doses promptly.
- Parents should keep unvaccinated children away from daycare, schools and crowded indoor settings during an outbreak.
- If you suspect measles, call ahead to a healthcare facility to prevent exposure to others.
- Maintain routine hygiene measures: cover coughs, practice good hand hygiene and improve indoor ventilation when possible.

Public health response and resources
Health departments typically respond with targeted vaccination drives, public information campaigns and coordination with schools and healthcare providers. Residents should follow local health department guidance, attend community vaccination events, and use official public health websites for the latest case counts and clinic locations.

While measles can be severe, especially for infants and immunocompromised people, timely vaccination and sensible precautions substantially reduce risk. If you have questions about vaccine eligibility or exposure management, contact your local health department or primary care provider.
